blocks.en: We designed hands-on lessons around plant stress, climate change, sustainability, and synthetic biology. After each lesson, we refined them through student questions, surveys, and educator feedback, creating a two-way exchange rather than a one-way lesson. Through hands-on plant experiments and games, students were encouraged to connect synthetic biology to the future of sustainable farming. To make the work reproducible, we documented our activities and created open-access lesson plans, games, and workshop materials that other students and educators can reuse and adapt.

blocks.en: In the process of developing our education lessons and events, we realized that it was important for people to have the ability to access our lessons and other resources in order to create a truly sustainable form of education. Driven by this thought, we decided to create a website of our own where students and teachers can download our lesson plans, slides and games for free. In total, we have uploaded three lesson plans, three slide decks, two card games, two online games and a plant stress simulator, free online. By transforming our materials into open-access tools, we aim to extend our reach beyond one-time workshops and empower communities to explore and teach about synthetic biology and our projects independently.

blocks.en: Overview

blocks.en: Designing an effective educational lesson requires moving from big ideas to a smooth, classroom-ready reality. Before stepping into a classroom, our team dedicated significant time to carefully planning, testing, and refining our educational content. We wanted to make sure our synthetic biology concepts were not only accurate and age-appropriate, but also engaging, safe, and easy for teachers. This phase outlines the process we used to transform complex scientific concepts into hands-on learning experiences for students across all age groups.

blocks.en: 1 · Lesson Plan Development
blocks.text: 1 · Lesson Plan Development
blocks.zh: 1 · 教案發展

blocks.en: Before we started designing, we split the work so each team member focused on a single age group: elementary, junior high, or high school. This approach ensured every lesson plan received dedicated attention, allowing us to tailor the scientific depth, vocabulary, and teaching methods specifically to that age group’s learning capabilities. Next, we brainstormed the type of activities and content best suited for each group. We focused on keeping core synthetic biology, plant biology, and sustainability concepts consistent and present throughout all age groups while introducing aspects of iGEM and the project we were working on. We then scaled the complexity and depth of these details depending on the target age group. Other than just including things we felt were important, we also took the time to verify whether the content we were planning to teach was already covered in schools, ensuring our lessons didn't just repeat classroom material, but instead introduced fresh ideas to inspire students and spark their interest in new areas.

blocks.en: 4 · Run-through Sessions
blocks.text: 4 · Run-through Sessions
blocks.zh: 4 · 演練場次

blocks.en: Once school dates were confirmed, we assigned team members to each session. We then divided the slides and tasks so everyone could present topics they knew best. About a week before each event, we held full practice runs to simulate a real classroom setting and keep everyone on track. During these run-throughs, we also tested our games and experiments to fix any issues and ensure everything ran smoothly on the day of the event. Using these sessions helped us check whether the lesson plan contents and time allocation for each section were appropriate for the age group we were teaching.

blocks.en: In the world we live in nowadays, synthetic biology and other related areas are often associated with negative perceptions due to misconceptions surrounding the topic. As a result heated debates surrounding genetic engineering and biotechnology erupted with some questioning the morals and safety of continuing this practice. Additionally, students have limited opportunities to learn about synthetic biology, climate change, and sustainability through engaging, age-appropriate educational experiences. After recognizing this gap, we sought to provide students of all ages and the public with educational experiences that foster and encourage informed discussions about synthetic biology and its real-world applications. Lastly, throughout our events, sustainability and the development of reusable educational materials have also been a central focus in both the planning and execution of our educational activities.

blocks.en: To achieve the goals set above, we thoughtfully designed events that revolved around age-appropriate and interactive learning experiences that could actively engage students in learning about simplified biological concepts and thinking about the implications of synthetic biology to the world around them. blocks.en: However, we realized that learning goes both ways and that in order to bring the best experiences to those around us, we had to continue to evaluate ourselves and make improvements on our end. All the data collected was used to help better our program for subsequent events.

blocks.en: We then moved on to conducting a simple experiment that allowed students to really visualize what photosynthesis would look like in real time. The students were thrilled and in awe to watch tiny spinach leaf disks, initially sunk at the bottom of a beaker, slowly float to the surface as they generated oxygen under a light source. To connect back to the core idea of our project, we introduced heat as a variable in the experiment, this was done by replacing the room-temperature water with warmer water. As a result of this, the flotation process slowed down significantly or even stopped, showing the students that excessive heat can damage plant enzymes and hinder photosynthesis. Throughout the experiment, students were given worksheets that encouraged them to record experiment results as well as to discuss the results of the experiment with team members.

blocks.en: Introduction

blocks.en: To start off our lesson, we begin with introducing climate change and plant stresses. We begin by addressing the different types of stresses there are. For example, we mention high temperatures, droughts, flooding, and pests/diseases. As most students are familiar with the different types of plant stresses, we introduce the two terms biotic and abiotic. After, we introduce ways plants can defend against the varying stresses, for example, closing the stomata or producing stress-hormone responses.

blocks.en: Experiment
blocks.text: Experiment
blocks.zh: 實驗

blocks.en: We then moved into a hands-on experiment designed to let students actually watch photosynthesis happen in real time. Using spinach leaf disks that initially sank to the bottom of a beaker, students observed with excitement as the disks slowly rose to the surface, propelled by the oxygen bubbles they produced under a light source. To tie the experiment back to our project's central theme, we introduced heat as a variable by swapping the room-temperature water for warmer water. This caused the flotation process to slow dramatically or stop altogether, giving students a clear, visual demonstration that excess heat damages plant enzymes and disrupts photosynthesis. Throughout the activity, students used worksheets to record their observations and discuss their findings with teammates.

blocks.en: Card Game
blocks.text: Card Game
blocks.zh: 卡牌遊戲

blocks.en: To make the lesson more fun, we also created a card game that enables the students to really understand the effects of stress on plants. Each round begins by spinning the wheel to reveal a stress. All players then simultaneously check their hands, laying cards face-up if they hold a valid combo (a Sensor plus an Action card matching the revealed stress, with an optional Boost card). Players who form a valid combo are safe and discard those cards, while players who cannot may play a Functional card to steal or swap cards from a teammate who already succeeded. Anyone still without a valid combo after that receives one disaster token, and the next round begins.

blocks.en: Lastly, to end our lesson, we asked the students to participate in a debate. Currently, using synthetic biology on plants is a major debate throughout society, so through this activity students get to understand why exactly synthetic biology is controversial. Students split into two teams, Supporting (in favor of synthetic biology) and Opposing (against it), and are given 8 minutes to prepare their arguments. Each team selects 3 speakers, who take turns presenting in order, discussing for 45 seconds as a team before each turn and then speaking individually for 2 minutes. The first speaker lays out their team's evidence and reasoning, the second rebuts the opposing team's first speaker using their own team's evidence and reasoning, and the third summarizes the round and explains why their side should be favored over the opponent's.

blocks.en: Through our education program, we introduced junior high school students to plant stress, photosynthesis, climate change, and synthetic biology through a combination of interactive lessons, hands-on experiments, games, and debates. The spinach leaf-disk experiment provided students with a visual demonstration of how heat can affect photosynthesis, while the card game and debate encouraged them to apply synthetic biology concepts and consider different perspectives on its use in agriculture. Pre- and post-education surveys allowed us to evaluate changes in students’ knowledge, attitudes, and intended practices. Overall, the program successfully combined scientific learning with active participation, while student feedback highlighted the need to reduce lecture time, expand interactive activities, and provide additional visual support for difficult concepts such as DNA base pairing. These findings will guide us in improving future workshops and making our education program more engaging and accessible.

blocks.en: While waiting for the onion to fully immerse in the salt solution, we prepared a short video that demonstrates and visualizes photosynthesis. blocks.en: To help students better understand the processes of transcription, translation, and mutation in a more engaging and interactive way, we organized a game in which students worked together to pass a genetic sequence down the line. Students were given one of three different roles: the Sighter, Messenger, and Builder. The Sighter transcribed a DNA sequence and passed the transcribed sequence to the next student. The Messenger passed down the sequence to the next person. The Builder translated the sequence received from the student behind them. After the Builder wrote down their answer, each group checked their answers with the answer key. Through this interactive game, students can picture how genetic information is transcribed and translated more easily and understand how changes or errors in the sequence can lead to mutations.

After the Builder wrote down their answer, each group checked their answers with the answer key. Through this interactive game, students can picture how genetic information is transcribed and translated more easily and understand how changes or errors in the sequence can lead to mutations.

blocks.en: Lastly, we introduced the students to how engineered mutations can enhance plant protectant release in order to maximize extracellular protectant release while maintaining bacterial viability. In this section, we explained how different mutations target different components of the stress-responsive system to enhance protectant release through three distinct mechanisms: increase receptor sensitivity to the stress signal, engineer the export protein, and modify the protectant molecule for improved membrane permeability. We also explained the trade-offs that need to be considered to balance protectant release efficiency with bacterial viability, as overproduction may place additional stress on the bacteria and reduce their overall viability.

In these questions we covered topics such as plant stress, impact of drought, climate & environmental causes, molecular biology, project mechanics, synthetic biology foundations, and agricultural applications. Following the lesson, every category demonstrated marked knowledge growth. Post-survey accuracy reached 80% across most core areas, including Plant Stress, Climate & Environmental Causal Chains, Project Mechanics, and Synthetic Biology Foundations, while scores on Molecular Biology increased to 30%. Overall, these findings highlight the overall effectiveness of the educational intervention across all covered concepts.

blocks.en: The clearest piece of critical feedback centered on pacing: students noted that portions of the direct instruction “went on a bit too long,” pointing to lecture style teaching segments as the weak link relative to the hands-on activities. This pacing concern is reinforced by the case studies. Even a high-performing student who scored perfectly across the knowledge benchmarks deemed the lecture length as a drawback, indicating that stronger students in particular need less review time and faster transitions into applied, game-based learning. On the knowledge side, DNA base-pairing remained the toughest concept to land: despite a meaningful jump from a 0% pre-test baseline to 30% post-test accuracy, it was the one area where a student was observed making a direct conceptual error (matching ATCG to itself rather than its complement TAGC), signaling that this topic needs a more hands-on teaching method rather than passive explanation alone.

blocks.en: Overview

blocks.en: Education, in our eyes, isn't only about sharing information and teaching at one specific point of time, instead, it should be something that students are able to carry forward with them and continue to share and find useful over a period of time. Our education program focuses on helping students understand plant stress, climate change, sustainability, and synthetic biology through hands-on activities and interactive learning. However, we also wanted to consider what would happen after our lessons were finished. This is why throughout our education journey, one of our major goals was to create an education that was truly sustainable.

blocks.en: Mutual Learning and Dialogue
blocks.text: Mutual Learning and Dialogue

blocks.en: Our Education was implemented in a way where both sides were mutually able to contribute to the conversation rather than just a one way lecture. After each activity, students filled in a feedback survey. Their answers about climate change and synthetic biology guided our next lesson. For example, in Trial 2, a teacher asked how the planter linked to the topic, so we made sure to manage our time better in order to allow for more time to explain before we started moving. Furthermore, some students in Trial 1 explained that they felt like more support during the experiments would be more helpful, which is why we made sure to implement a strict 1:5 teacher to student ratio to make sure all students received the help they needed. In all, the feedback of teachers and students helped to shape how we conducted future school outreach events.

blocks.en: Our educational rollout followed a deliberate, multi-stage process that began with assessing audience needs and language requirements, leading to bilingual (English and Traditional Chinese) materials. blocks.en: Environmental Sustainability
blocks.text: Environmental Sustainability

blocks.en: Our education program focuses on helping students understand environmental challenges and their connection to plants, agriculture, and climate change. Through our lessons and activities on plant stress, students explore how factors such as extreme heat, drought, salinity, and disease can affect plants and food production. By introducing these topics at a young age, we hope to build greater awareness of environmental challenges and encourage students to think about how science and technology can contribute to a more sustainable future.

attrs.en: Survey analysis by age group
attrs.zh: 依學齡層的問卷分析

attrs.en: Seven small bar charts, one per knowledge question, comparing pre-survey and post-survey percentage correct for the preliminary trial and trials 1 to 3.
attrs.zh: 七張小型長條圖，每一題知識題一張，比較前測與後測的正確率百分比，涵蓋先行試教與第 1 至 3 次試教。

attrs.en: Horizontal bar chart of the seven knowledge questions, pre-survey against post-survey, combined across all trials; every post-survey bar is higher.
attrs.zh: 七題知識題的橫向長條圖，前測對後測，合併所有試教場次；每一條後測長條都比前測高。

attrs.en: Radar chart with eight axes, A to H, plotting the percentage of yes responses for each of the four trials as overlaid outlines; the trial 3 outline reaches furthest on every axis.
attrs.zh: 雷達圖，八條軸 A 到 H，以疊合的輪廓線呈現四次試教各自回答「是」的百分比；第 3 次試教的輪廓在每一條軸上都伸得最遠。

attrs.en: Stacked horizontal bars showing disagree, neutral and agree proportions for four action and intent statements.
attrs.zh: 堆疊橫條圖，呈現四項行動與意願陳述的不同意、中立與同意比例。

attrs.en: Stacked horizontal bars showing disagree, neutral and agree proportions for four attitude and sentiment statements.
attrs.zh: 堆疊橫條圖，呈現四項態度與情感陳述的不同意、中立與同意比例。

attrs.en: Horizontal bar chart comparing pre-survey and post-survey percentage correct for seven junior high knowledge questions; DNA base pairing rises from 0 to 30 percent, the others finish between 70 and 90 percent.
attrs.zh: 橫向長條圖，比較國中七題知識題的前測與後測正確率百分比；DNA 鹼基配對從 0 升到 30%，其餘各題落在 70% 到 90% 之間。

attrs.en: Stacked horizontal bars showing disagree, neutral and agree proportions for six attitude categories, A to F; only eco-awareness (D) has any disagreement.
attrs.zh: 堆疊橫條圖，呈現六個態度類別 A 到 F 的不同意、中立與同意比例；只有環保意識（D）出現不同意。

attrs.en: Stacked horizontal bars showing disagree, neutral and agree proportions for willingness to act (G) and continued ag-tech engagement (H).
attrs.zh: 堆疊橫條圖，呈現行動意願（G）與持續接觸農業科技（H）的不同意、中立與同意比例。

attrs.en: Horizontal bar chart of correct responses out of 28 for six high school knowledge questions, pre-survey against post-survey; every question rises and every post-survey bar is at 22 or more.
attrs.zh: 橫向長條圖，呈現高中六題知識題在 28 份作答中的答對數，前測對後測；每一題都上升，每一條後測長條都在 22 以上。

attrs.en: Stacked horizontal bars showing disagree, neutral and agree proportions for four action statements: notice weather, consider major, share what I learned, open to applications.
attrs.zh: 堆疊橫條圖，呈現四項行動陳述的不同意、中立與同意比例：注意天氣、考慮相關科系、分享所學、對相關應用保持開放。

attrs.en: Stacked horizontal bars showing disagree, neutral and agree proportions for five attitude statements: solve real-life problems, concerned about crop yield, pay attention to products, lesson interesting, learn more lessons.
attrs.zh: 堆疊橫條圖，呈現五項態度陳述的不同意、中立與同意比例：解決真實生活中的問題、關心作物產量、注意相關產品、課程有趣、想上更多這樣的課。

attrs.en: Card titled NaD1 Defensin in Chinese, an action card for biotic stress showing a shield crossed by two swords.
attrs.zh: 卡片名稱為中文的「NaD1 防禦素」，是對應生物性逆境的行動卡，圖案是一面盾牌交叉著兩把劍。

attrs.en: Card titled Performance Enhancer in Chinese, a boost card showing a lightning bolt inside a sun.
attrs.zh: 卡片名稱為中文的「效能強化」，是一張加成卡，圖案是太陽裡的一道閃電。

attrs.en: Card titled Pathogen Sensor in Chinese, a sensor card showing two spotted mushrooms.
attrs.zh: 卡片名稱為中文的「病原感測器」，是一張感測器卡，圖案是兩朵有斑點的蘑菇。

attrs.en: Card titled My Good Friend in Chinese, a functional card showing two hands shaking.
attrs.zh: 卡片名稱為中文的「我的好朋友」，是一張功能卡，圖案是兩隻握在一起的手。

attrs.en: Card titled Pest Sensor in Chinese, a sensor card showing a beetle, a caterpillar and a ladybird on a chewed leaf.
attrs.zh: 卡片名稱為中文的「害蟲感測器」，是一張感測器卡，圖案是一片被啃過的葉子上有甲蟲、毛毛蟲與瓢蟲。

attrs.en: Card titled Heat Sensor in Chinese, a sensor card showing a sun beside a thermometer, triggered above 33 degrees Celsius.
attrs.zh: 卡片名稱為中文的「高溫感測器」，是一張感測器卡，圖案是太陽與溫度計，在 33 °C 以上觸發。

attrs.en: CropShield’s opening screen: the game title in neon over a dark field, with iPad or mobile and PC or laptop control options and a Continue button.
attrs.zh: CropShield 的開場畫面：霓虹字的遊戲標題浮在深色田地上，提供 iPad 或手機、PC 或筆電兩種操作選項，下方有「繼續」按鈕。

attrs.en: The setup screen: four ReLEAFamon starters on the left with their specialities, three Distressamon on the right, and a Start Battle button below.
attrs.zh: 設定畫面：左側是四隻 ReLEAFamon 初始角色與各自的專長，右側是三隻 Distressamon，下方是「開始戰鬥」按鈕。

attrs.en: A battle in progress: a green ReLEAFamon faces an orange Distressamon in a pixel-art scene, with health bars above and the action menu, gather, photosynthesise, moves, engineer and market, on the right.
attrs.zh: 戰鬥進行中：像素風場景裡一隻綠色的 ReLEAFamon 對上一隻橘色的 Distressamon，上方是生命條，右側是行動選單：採集、光合作用、招式、工程與市場。

attrs.en: The simulator on day 1: a healthy tomato seedling marked Growing Well on the left, the five environmental sliders on the right.
attrs.zh: 模擬器在第 1 天：左側是一株健康的番茄苗，標示「生長良好」，右側是五個環境滑桿。

attrs.en: The same simulator under combined stress: the seedling is wilted and marked Multiple Stresses, with temperature at 40 degrees, water at 25 percent and sunlight at 21 hours.
attrs.zh: 同一個模擬器在複合逆境下：苗已經枯萎，標示「多重逆境」，溫度 40 度、水分 25%、日照 21 小時。
